boxplots-s1.title: Commute times of 20 nurses

plot.label: Boxplot of the commute times of 20 nurses in minutes, with the box from 13.5 to 27, the median at 19.5, whiskers from 6 to 37 and one outlier at 58

boxplots-s1.text: The one-way commute times, in minutes, of 20 nurses at a clinic, in order: 6, 9, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 31, 34, 37, 58 (invented data). The boxplot is drawn from these values.

boxplots-s2.title: Final exam scores
boxplots-s2.text: The five-number summary of the final exam scores of 120 students (invented data).

items.q: What is the first quartile, $Q_1$, of the commute times, in minutes?

why.correct: Lower half: the 10 smallest values, 6 to 19. Its median is $\frac{13 + 14}{2} = 13.5$ minutes.

mistakes.why: That is the 5th value. The lower half has 10 values, so $Q_1$ is the average of its 5th and 6th values: (13 + 14)/2.
That is the median of all 20 values. $Q_1$ is the median of the lower half.

items.q: What is the upper fence, $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$, in minutes?

mistakes.why: That adds just one IQR to $Q_3$. The fence adds $1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 1.5(13.5) = 20.25$.
That uses the range, 52, instead of the IQR, 13.5.

items.q: Why does the right whisker end at 37 minutes and not at the maximum, 58?

why.correct: Whiskers go to the most extreme values that are not outliers. Outliers, beyond the fences, are marked separately.
options: The whisker stops at an actual data value, the largest one inside the fence.
Right: a whisker reaches the most extreme value inside the fences, here 37; 58 is above 47.25.
Whiskers can have different lengths; that is how a boxplot shows skew.
Whiskers are not set at a percentile; they end at the most extreme value inside the fences.
Whiskers stop at $Q_3$ plus the IQR, which is about 40.5
58 is beyond the upper fence, so it is drawn as an outlier
The whisker is drawn to the same length as the left whisker
37 is the 95th percentile of the 20 commute times

items.q: About what percent of the nurses have commutes longer than $Q_3$, 27 minutes?

why.correct: The five numbers split the data into quarters: about 25% of the values lie above $Q_3$. Here 5 of 20 nurses do.
options: About 75% are at or below $Q_3$; the part above is a quarter.
The box holds the middle half; the upper whisker and outliers hold about a quarter.
The outlier is one of five values above 27 minutes.
Right: $Q_3$ has about three quarters of the data at or below it, so about a quarter above.
About 75%, the percent above the box
About 50%, the percent inside the box
About 5%, since just one nurse is an outlier
About 25%

items.q: A student says, "The boxplot shows that the commute times have one peak." What is wrong with this claim?

why.correct: Never read modality (one peak, two peaks) from a boxplot. Use a dotplot or histogram for shape details.
options: Right: a boxplot hides how values are spread inside the box and whiskers, so it cannot show modality, gaps or clusters.
A boxplot shows no peaks at all; the halves of the box are quarters of the data, not peaks.
Commute times are quantitative. The issue is what a boxplot can show.
An outlier is a single far value, not a peak.
A boxplot shows five numbers and outliers, so it cannot show peaks
The boxplot shows two peaks, one on each side of the median
Commute times are categorical, so they have no peaks
The peak of a boxplot is the outlier at 58 minutes

items.q: Would a boxplot of these scores show any outliers?

why.correct: $\text{IQR} = 79 - 63 = 16$; fences at $63 - 1.5(16) = 39$ and $79 + 1.5(16) = 103$. The min and max are inside, so the whiskers reach 41 and 98.
options: Far below the median is not enough; 41 is above the lower fence of 39.
98 is below the upper fence of 103, so it is not an outlier.
Right: $\text{IQR} = 16$, so the fences are $63 - 24 = 39$ and $79 + 24 = 103$. The minimum 41 and maximum 98 are inside.
The $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule needs only $Q_1$ and $Q_3$, and the extremes.
Yes: the score of 41 is far below the median of 72
Yes: the score of 98 is far above the third quartile of 79
No: the fences are 39 and 103, and every score is between them
It is impossible to decide without the mean and standard deviation

items.q: About how many of the 120 students scored between 63 and 79?

why.correct: The box spans the middle 50% of the data: about $0.5 \times 120 = 60$ students.
options: A quarter lies in each whisker section; the box holds two quarters.
About three quarters scored 79 or less; between 63 and 79 is the middle half.
Right: the box, from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, holds the middle half of the data: about half of 120.
16 points is the width of the box, not a count of students.
About 30, a quarter of the students
About 90, three quarters of the students
About 60
About 16, the IQR of the scores

items.q: A student scored 85. What can you say about this score?

why.correct: 85 lies between $Q_3 = 79$ and the maximum 98, the top quarter of the scores.
options: Right: 85 is above $Q_3 = 79$, so it is higher than about 75% of the scores.
Values above $Q_3$ are ordinary parts of the data; 85 is well inside the upper fence of 103.
The median is 72. The middle of the min and max is not the median.
The box ends at 79; 85 is beyond it.
It is in the top quarter of the scores
It is an outlier, since it is above the third quartile
It is near the median, since it is near the middle of 41 and 98
It is in the middle half of the scores, inside the box

items.q: Which statement compares the spread of the lower and upper quarters of the scores?

why.correct: Each quarter holds the same number of values; a wider section means those values are more spread out. Here 63 − 41 = 22 and 98 − 79 = 19.
options: Each quarter holds about 30 students; the quarters differ in width, not in count.
Equal counts do not mean equal widths: 22 points against 19.
Reaching the maximum is not the same as being wide: 79 to 98 is 19 points.
Right: 22 points against 19 points, so the lowest quarter of scores is more spread out.
The top quarter has more students than the lowest quarter
The two quarters are equally spread, as each holds a quarter of the scores
The top quarter is more spread out, since it reaches the highest score
The lowest quarter (41 to 63) is more spread out than the top quarter (79 to 98)

items.q: What is the five-number summary of 3, 5, 7, 8, 12, 13, 14?

why.correct: Min 3; $Q_1$ = median of 3, 5, 7 = 5; median 8; $Q_3$ = median of 12, 13, 14 = 13; max 14.
options: That keeps the median, 8, in both halves. With n odd, leave it out: lower half 3, 5, 7.
Right: median 8; the lower half 3, 5, 7 has median 5; the upper half 12, 13, 14 has median 13.
8.86 is the mean. The five-number summary uses the median, 8.
The quartiles are the medians of each half, not the neighbors of the median.
3, 6, 8, 12.5, 14, with the median kept in both halves
3, 5, 8.86, 13, 14, using the mean for the center
3, 7, 8, 12, 14, using the values next to the median

why.correct: Leave out the median, 8. The upper half is 12, 13, 14, so $Q_3 = 13$.

mistakes.why: That keeps the median, 8, in the upper half (8, 12, 13, 14). With n odd, leave the median out: the median of 12, 13, 14 is 13.
That is the value just above the median. $Q_3$ is the median of the upper half.

items.q: What does the length of the box in a boxplot show?

why.correct: The box spans $Q_1$ to $Q_3$, so its length is the IQR.
options: Right: the box runs from $Q_1$ to $Q_3$.
The range runs from the end of one whisker (or outlier) to the other.
A boxplot uses quartiles, not the mean or standard deviation.
A boxplot does not show how many values there are.
The IQR, the spread of the middle half of the data
The range, from the minimum value to the maximum value
The mean plus and minus one standard deviation
The number of values in the data set

items.q: Data on wait times have $Q_1 = 4$ and $Q_3 = 10$ minutes. The three largest values are 17, 18 and 22 minutes. Where does the right whisker of the boxplot end?

why.correct: $\text{IQR} = 6$, so the upper fence is $10 + 1.5(6) = 19$. The whisker goes to the largest value at or below 19, which is 18; 22 is marked as an outlier.
options: 22 is above the upper fence of 19, so it is drawn as an outlier, not reached by the whisker.
A whisker ends at an actual data value, not at the fence.
Right: the upper fence is $10 + 1.5(6) = 19$. 22 is beyond it, so 22 is an outlier and the whisker stops at 18, the largest value inside the fence.
The box ends at $Q_3$; the whisker continues past it to the largest value inside the fence.
At 22 minutes, the largest value in the data
At 19 minutes, the upper fence itself
At 18 minutes
At 10 minutes, the third quartile of the wait times

items.q: In a boxplot, the median is close to $Q_1$ and the right whisker is much longer than the left. What is the most likely shape?

why.correct: Long right whisker and the median near $Q_1$: the upper values are spread out, so the distribution is skewed right.
options: A median near $Q_1$ means the lower values are bunched, and the upper values stretch out to the right.
Right: the upper half of the data stretches farther, a long tail toward the larger values.
Symmetry would show a median near the middle of the box and whiskers of similar length.
A boxplot cannot show peaks.
Skewed left, since the median is on the left of the box
Skewed right
Roughly symmetric, since there is one box
Bimodal, with one peak in the box and one in the whisker

items.q: Which feature of a distribution can a boxplot show? Select all that apply.

why.correct: A boxplot shows the five-number summary and outliers; it hides peaks, gaps and the mean.
options: Right: they are marked as separate points.
The box and whiskers hide peaks, so a boxplot cannot show modality.
A boxplot shows the median, not the mean.
Gaps inside the box or a whisker are hidden.
Outliers by the $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$ rule
Whether the distribution has two peaks
The mean of the data
Gaps between clusters of values

items.q: A boxplot of 40 test scores has its median line in the middle of the box and two whiskers of equal length. Which conclusion is justified?

why.correct: Equal box halves and whiskers mean the quarters of the data are equally spread on each side of the median: roughly symmetric, as far as a boxplot can tell.
options: A boxplot cannot show peaks; the scores could even be bimodal.
A boxplot does not show the mean, so this cannot be read from it.
Each of the four sections holds about a quarter of the scores.
Right: that is what equal halves of the box and equal whiskers show; the distribution looks roughly symmetric.
The distribution of the scores has exactly one peak
The mean of the scores is exactly equal to the median
Each quarter of the box holds twice as many scores as a whisker
The quarters of the data are spread evenly on both sides of the median
